+# Access management
+
+**Collection and storage.** Credentials are entered through a private HTTPS vault
+form authenticated with Slack. Requests are bound to the workspace, member, task,
+and website origin. Secrets are encrypted in the local vault; its encryption key
+is stored on the same host, so the host operator remains trusted.
+
+**Use and reuse.** Clanker receives credential handles and metadata. The backend
+passes the selected secret to Composio's Browser Tool separately from task text,
+after checking its reported HTTPS origin. Saved credentials and requester-scoped
+browser sessions support reuse. An optional saved TOTP key supplies authenticator
+codes; SMS/email codes use private, single-use forms, and device approvals remain
+manual. Saving TOTP alongside the password reduces separation between factors.
+
+**Sharing.** Owners invite a Slack member to use selected credentials. Invitations
+grant neither the whole vault nor onward sharing, and newly saved credentials are
+not automatically included. Membership and grants are checked at use time.
+Sharing a login inherits that website account's permissions; it does not create
+read-only access. Shared cards still require the owner's approval for each bound
+checkout.
+
+**Revocation.** Revoking an invitation denies further credential use and cancels
+pending handoffs. If it was used in a browser, the recipient's affected context
+stays blocked until cleanup succeeds. The hosted Browser Tool cannot confirm
+cookie deletion, so operator cleanup may be required. Stopping a browser task is
+not website logout, and an existing website session may remain active.
+
+**Trust and improvements.** Composio receives the selected login secret and may
+retain request data. Origin checks depend on provider reports. Encryption does
+not protect against a compromised host or browser provider. The next improvements
+are verifiable provider-side session deletion and narrower permissions for
+delegated actions.

content.text:
A **credential handle is an ID pointing to a saved credential**, like `vault_a1b2c3d4e5f6`.

Clanker can say “use this saved Gmail login” by passing that ID. The backend checks access, retrieves the password, and supplies it to the browser.

The ID contains no password, and knowing it alone doesn’t grant access.
